claim: the dispatch log line's webhooks= field records whether envelope.type is in WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES rather than whether any delivery rows were actually created.
deliver backs off with the blocking time.sleep(delay) inside an async coroutine, stalling the event loop and every other gathered delivery for the duration.
_claim_batch returns ORM rows loaded inside with session_scope(), so later attribute reads in deliver and send_once touch detached, expired instances.
_acquire_lock reads LOCK_KEY and then sets it as separate operations, so two workers that both observe an empty key both acquire the lock.
_claim_batch selects pending rows with no FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and no conditional update, so concurrent claimers can select and deliver the same rows.
rows flipped to in_flight by _claim_batch are moved on only by _finish and nothing resets stale in_flight rows, so a crash or unhandled exception strands them outside the pending query permanently.

retry state is held in the local attempt counter and attempts/next_attempt_at are written only by the terminal _finish, so progress is lost across restarts and the next_attempt_at schedule is never used.
deliver treats every response outside 200-299 as retryable and re-POSTs it up to MAX_ATTEMPTS, so a 4xx is retried instead of being marked permanent immediately.
backoff_for returns exactly BASE_DELAY_SECONDS ** attempt seconds with no randomisation, so there is no jitter and deliveries failing together retry at the same instants.
enqueue_for_event writes next_attempt_at=datetime.utcnow(), a naive value, while _claim_batch compares against the aware datetime.now(timezone.utc).
_finish assigns row.status immediately after session.get without a None check, raising AttributeError when the delivery row no longer exists.
asyncio.gather is called without return_exceptions=True, so the first delivery to raise propagates out and its sibling coroutines are abandoned.
batch is assigned only inside the try while if not batch is evaluated after the try/finally, so a failure in _claim_batch can reach the test with batch unbound.
the delivery AsyncClient is constructed with follow_redirects=True, so a receiver can redirect the signed payload and its signature headers to another host.
send_once logs the full header dict at INFO, writing the X-Acme-Signature and timestamp values into application logs on every attempt.
_finish stores the remote response.text in response_body with no truncation or size bound, so a receiver controls how much content is persisted per attempt.
enqueue_for_event, _claim_batch and _finish perform blocking synchronous SQLAlchemy work while called from coroutines, so every database round trip stalls the event loop.
the POSTed body is the bare event payload with no event_id or event_type in the body or headers, so a receiver has no id to deduplicate on.
dispatch gates the webhook enqueue on the hardcoded three-entry WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES set, so an endpoint subscribed to any other type, or to all types via an empty event_types, receives nothing.
the except Exception around enqueue_for_event logs a warning and lets dispatch return the event id as success, so a failed enqueue drops the webhook with no retry or failure signal.
the event row is committed when session_scope exits and enqueue_for_event then opens its own transaction, so a failure between the two leaves a persisted event with no delivery rows.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_webhook_deliveries_event on webhook_deliveries (event_id) permits only one delivery row per event, so fan-out to a second endpoint violates the index and the whole enqueue fails.
_finish writes the status failed_permanent, which the migration's CHECK constraint ('pending','in_flight','delivered','failed') does not allow, so a permanent failure cannot be recorded.
the migration adds organizations.webhooks_enabled NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE but no code in the change reads it, so the flag has no effect on endpoint creation or delivery.
the only index available to the claim query is on status, while _claim_batch also filters on and orders by next_attempt_at, so the pending set is sorted on every poll.
no index supports list_deliveries, which filters on endpoint_id and orders by created_at DESC with neither column indexed.
the migration contains only forward DDL with no down or rollback section, so the two new tables and the organizations column cannot be reverted by the migration tool.
WebhookEndpoint.to_dict includes signing_secret, so GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints returns every endpoint's signing secret rather than exposing it only in the creation response.
models.py declares created_at, updated_at and next_attempt_at as DateTime(timezone=True) while migration 0042 creates them as TIMESTAMP without time zone, so offsets are dropped on write.
the STATUSES tuple is referenced by no column, validator, or check, and lists failed_permanent where the migration's CHECK lists failed.
WebhookDelivery.updated_at has a creation default but no onupdate, so writes that do not go through _finish, such as the in_flight flip, leave the timestamp stale.
WebhookDelivery.event_type is declared String(100) in the model while the migration creates the column as unbounded TEXT.

_claim_batch orders by next_attempt_at and list_deliveries orders by created_at, both non-unique wall-clock timestamps with no unique tie-break ahead of the LIMIT, so the order among tied rows is undefined.
run_worker's poll body wraps _claim_batch, asyncio.gather and the Redis calls in a try whose only clause is finally, so any exception propagates out of the while True loop and terminates the worker.
endpoint.active is filtered only in enqueue_for_event and is re-checked in neither _claim_batch nor deliver, so rows queued before an endpoint was deactivated are still POSTed to it.
enqueue_for_event is declared async but contains no await, so its coroutine signature promises a yield to the event loop that never happens.
deliver opens its own session and re-fetches the endpoint by primary key for every delivery, so a batch of 100 issues 100 single-row lookups for what is typically a handful of distinct endpoints.
WebhookDelivery.to_dict returns next_attempt_at but omits created_at and updated_at, so a caller has no timestamp for when an attempt actually happened.
webhook_deliveries stores a full copy of every event payload and the full remote response_body with no retention policy, TTL, purge job, or size bound.
migration 0042 combines the two CREATE TABLE statements with an ALTER TABLE on the existing organizations table, so a lock wait or failure on that hot table rolls back the whole feature's schema.
webhook_deliveries.endpoint_id is declared REFERENCES webhook_endpoints (id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting an endpoint destroys its entire delivery history.
webhook_endpoints has no index on org_id, the column both list_webhook_endpoints and enqueue_for_event filter on.
None of the three new routes create_webhook_endpoint, list_webhook_endpoints and list_deliveries carries a rate-limit dependency or decorator, so each is callable without any per-caller throttle.

list_deliveries orders by WebhookDelivery.created_at with no unique tie-break before applying limit, and rows written by one enqueue_for_event fan-out share that timestamp, so which rows fall inside the cut is undefined among ties.
serialize calls json.dumps pinning only sort_keys, leaving ensure_ascii and separators at the running Python's defaults, so the canonical signed form is not fully specified by the code.

docs/webhooks.md states several behaviours at once that the implementation in the same change does not have — https-only URL acceptance, a signing secret that cannot be read back, jittered backoff, immediate permanent failure on 4xx, a signature over the raw request body, and delivery of every subscribed event type.

the documented retry table lists four delays (2s, 4s, 8s, 16s) while MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5 implies a fifth attempt whose 32s wait is neither documented nor covered by test_backoff_grows_exponentially, which parametrizes only attempts 1-4.
test_backoff_grows_exponentially hardcodes its expected delays as literals instead of deriving them from BASE_DELAY_SECONDS.
the two coroutine tests are marked @pytest.mark.asyncio while the change adds neither a pytest-asyncio dependency nor an asyncio_mode configuration, so they may never actually run.

no query on the worker path carries an organization predicate, and deliver re-fetches the endpoint by delivery.endpoint_id without confirming it still belongs to the organization whose event produced the delivery.
the change depends on app.db.session_scope committing its writes and on its expire_on_commit setting, neither of which is part of the diff and so cannot be confirmed from it.
enqueue_for_event returns the number of delivery rows it created and dispatch discards that return value at the only call site.
webhook_deliveries.event_id is declared BIGINT NOT NULL with no foreign key to the events table, so the reference to events exists by convention only.

the new settings routes create_webhook_endpoint, list_webhook_endpoints and list_deliveries are declared async def while calling the synchronous session_scope and session.query, so the blocking database work runs on the event loop instead of the threadpool a def handler would have been given.

the change hand-rolls rate limiting, an outbound HTTP client and a signing-secret generator without establishing whether the repository already provides shared helpers of those kinds that the new code should have adopted instead.
the three new routes are annotated -> dict and -> list[dict] with no FastAPI response_model, so nothing constrains or filters the fields the handlers serialize into the response.
verify is exported and called by nothing in the change except the tests, so the reference verifier the docs point customers at has no production caller.
new_signing_secret builds a prefixed opaque token from scratch although the codebase's ApiKey model already carries a prefix column of that shape, so it may duplicate an existing token generator.

list_deliveries filters only on the endpoint_id taken from the path and never checks that the endpoint belongs to the caller's organization, so any authenticated user can read another organization's delivery rows.
create_webhook_endpoint performs no host validation, so a caller can register a loopback, link-local, or internal address that the delivery worker will then POST to from inside the network.

create_webhook_endpoint validates the URL with parsed.scheme.startswith("http"), which accepts plaintext http:// and any scheme merely beginning with those characters such as httpfoo://, contradicting the documented https-only rule.
the limit parameter is declared Query(50, ge=1) with no upper bound, so one request can pull an unbounded number of delivery rows.
event_types is persisted as an unconstrained list[str] with no membership check against the event types the system emits, so a misspelled or unknown name is accepted and silently never matches.
EndpointIn.url is a bare str with no length or format constraint, so an arbitrarily long string is accepted, stored, and later used as a request target.
nothing caps how many endpoints one organization can register, so a caller can multiply the per-event fan-out and delivery rows without limit.
list_webhook_endpoints calls .all() with no limit, offset, or pagination, so the response size grows with the number of endpoints in the org.
the change adds only create and read routes, so an endpoint cannot be deactivated, deleted, or have its signing secret rotated through the API.

sign HMACs json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True) while the request is sent with client.post(json=...), so the signed bytes differ from the transmitted body and a receiver hashing the raw request body cannot reproduce the signature.
sign MACs only the serialised payload, so the X-Acme-Timestamp header is unauthenticated and a replayer can rewrite it without invalidating the signature.
verify recomputes a fresh timestamp from time.time() and accepts no received timestamp, so it cannot enforce the documented five-minute freshness window.
verify compares digests with expected == signature instead of a constant-time comparison, so the comparison short-circuits on the first differing byte.
new_signing_secret builds the secret from random.choice, which draws on the non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister PRNG rather than a CSPRNG.
SECRET_BYTES = 32 is used as a character count over a 62-symbol alphabet, so the constant's name misstates the entropy of the secret it produces.
test_send_once_posts_the_signed_payload captures both the request body and the signature header but asserts only the sha256= prefix, never verifying the signature against the captured body.
deliver, _finish, _claim_batch, _acquire_lock, enqueue_for_event and run_worker have no tests; only the pure helpers and send_once are exercised.
test_verify_accepts_signature_produced_by_sign is tautological because verify calls sign internally, so the assertion holds for any implementation and pins nothing about the on-the-wire format.
the new HTTP routes create_webhook_endpoint, list_webhook_endpoints and list_deliveries have no tests, so the URL validation and org scoping are unexercised.
test_max_attempts_matches_documented_limit asserts MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5 against a literal and exercises no retry code, so it cannot fail for a behavioural reason.
test_new_signing_secret_has_prefix_and_length asserts only the prefix and length, which a predictable or constant generator satisfies exactly as well as a CSPRNG.
the tests substitute hand-rolled FakeEndpoint and FakeDelivery class-attribute stubs for the real ORM models, so detached-instance and missing-row behaviour is never exercised.
